function.description: Executes a system-level command using os.system() on Windows operating systems. It can execute single or multiple commands chained with '&&'. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

command.description: The system command to be executed. To execute multiple commands, separate them with '&&'. For example, 'dir && echo done'.

### What “CPU usage” actually means | Term | What it shows | Typical units | |------|---------------|---------------| | **CPU %** | The fraction of the processor’s total capacity that is being used at a given instant. 100 % means the CPU is fully busy. | Percent | | **Load average** (Linux) | The average number of runnable processes over 1‑, 5‑, and 15‑minute intervals. | Processes | | **Per‑core usage** | The same % value, but broken down for each logical core. | Percent | | **Idle time** | The portion of time the CPU spends doing nothing. | Percent | | **Wait time** | Time spent waiting for I/O (often shown as “% IOWait” on Linux). | Percent | > **Bottom line:** > *CPU usage* is a snapshot of how much of the CPU’s processing power is being consumed by running tasks. High values can mean a heavy workload, a runaway process, or background activity you didn’t expect. --- ## How to check CPU usage on common platforms | OS | Quick ways to view CPU usage | Command‑line alternatives | |----|------------------------------|---------------------------| | **Windows** | • **Task Manager** – `Ctrl+Shift+Esc` → “Performance” tab → “CPU” graph.
• **Resource Monitor** – “CPU” tab.
• **PowerShell** – `Get-Counter '\Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time'` | `wmic cpu get loadpercentage` | | **macOS** | • **Activity Monitor** – “CPU” tab.
• **Terminal** – `top -l 1 -n 0 | grep "CPU usage"` | `ps -A -o %cpu,comm | sort -k1 -r | head` | | **Linux** | • **top** or **htop** – real‑time per‑core view.
• **vmstat** – `vmstat 1` (shows %idle).
• **mpstat** – `mpstat -P ALL 1` (per‑core).
• **sar** – `sar -u 1` (requires sysstat). | `cat /proc/stat` (parse `cpu` line) | | **Android** | • **Developer options** → “Running services” or “CPU usage”.
• **ADB shell** – `top` or `dumpsys cpuinfo`. | `adb shell top -n 1` | | **iOS** | • **Xcode Instruments** – “CPU Profiler”.
• **Console** – `log show --predicate 'process == "YourApp"' --info`. | Not typically exposed via CLI. | --- ## Interpreting the numbers | Situation | What you see | Why it matters | |-----------|--------------|----------------| | **CPU % ≈ 0–10 %** | Light usage (idle or background tasks). | Normal for a desktop that’s mostly idle. | | **CPU % ≈ 10–50 %** | Moderate usage (web browsing, office apps). | Acceptable for most workloads. | | **CPU % ≈ 50–90 %** | Heavy usage (gaming, video encoding, data crunching). | May cause lag or heat if sustained. | | **CPU % ≈ 90–100 %** | Near‑max load (CPU‑bound program, malware loop, runaway process). | Can lead to sluggishness, overheating, or crashes. | | **Load average > #cores** (Linux) | More runnable processes than cores. | Indicates contention; may cause slowdowns. | | **High %IOWait** (Linux) | CPU idle because it’s waiting for disk/SSD. | Not a CPU problem; look at I/O subsystem. | --- ## Common causes of high CPU usage | Cause | Typical symptoms | Quick checks | |-------|------------------|--------------| | **Background services** (Windows Search, Indexing, Updates) | CPU spikes during idle periods | Task Manager → “Processes” tab | | **Antivirus scans** | CPU climbs when a scan starts | Antivirus UI or Task Manager | | **Malware / trojan** | Persistent high CPU, unknown processes | Run a full malware scan, check Task Manager | | **Infinite loops / bugs** | One process hogging CPU | Identify process, kill/restart | | **Heavy applications** (video editing, 3D rendering, games) | Sustained high CPU | Acceptable if you’re running them | | **Virtualization / containers** | Host CPU high due to guest workloads | Check VM/Container stats | | **Driver issues** | CPU spikes after driver install | Update or roll back drivers | | **Thermal throttling** | CPU usage drops after a while | Check temperatures (HWMonitor, iStat) | --- ## How to reduce unwanted CPU usage | Step | What to do | Why it helps | |------|------------|--------------| | 1. **Identify the culprit** | Open Task Manager / Activity Monitor / top and look for the process with the highest %CPU. | You need to know what’s causing the load. | | 2. **Disable startup programs** | Windows: `msconfig` or Settings → Apps → Startup. macOS: System Preferences → Users & Groups → Login Items. | Reduces background load. | | 3. **Check for malware** | Run Windows Defender, Malwarebytes, or your preferred scanner. | Removes malicious processes. | | 4. **Update drivers & OS** | Install latest updates. | Fixes known bugs that can cause high CPU. | | 5. **Adjust power settings** | Windows: Power Options → High Performance or Balanced. macOS: Energy Saver → “Prevent computer from sleeping”. | Prevents aggressive throttling that can misreport CPU usage. | | 6. **Limit background services** | Disable Windows Search, Superfetch (SysMain), or other services you don’t need. | Cuts unnecessary CPU cycles. | | 7. **Use lighter software** | Switch to a less CPU‑intensive editor, browser, or media player. | Reduces load. | | 8. **Upgrade hardware** | Add more RAM, switch to SSD, or upgrade CPU. | Gives more headroom for demanding tasks. | --- ## Quick command‑line snippets | OS | Command | What it prints | |----|---------|----------------| | **Windows PowerShell** | `Get-Counter '\Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time'` | Current overall CPU % | | **Windows CMD** | `wmic cpu get loadpercentage` | Current overall CPU % | | **Linux** | `top -bn1 | grep "Cpu(s)"` | CPU usage line (user, system, idle, iowait) | | **Linux** | `mpstat -P ALL 1 1` | Per‑core usage | | **macOS** | `top -l 1 -n 0 | grep "CPU usage"` | CPU usage line | | **macOS** | `ps -A -o %cpu,comm | sort -k1 -r | head` | Top 5 CPU‑hungry processes | --- ## Bottom line - **CPU usage** is a quick indicator of how busy your processor is. - **100 %** means the CPU is fully occupied; anything above ~70 % for long periods can be a sign of a problem (unless you’re running a CPU‑intensive task). - Use built‑in tools (Task Manager, Activity Monitor, top/htop) or simple command‑line commands to spot the culprit. - Once identified, you can disable background services, update drivers, scan for malware, or simply let the heavy application run. If you’re seeing a specific pattern (e.g., CPU spikes every 5 minutes) or a particular process that you can’t identify, let me know the OS and the process name, and I can help you dig deeper!
